q: Unknown A, C11H12O2, gives the IR, 1H NMR and 13C NMR (with DEPT) spectra shown. The 1H doublets at δ 7.68 and 6.44 share J = 16.0 Hz. What is the degree of unsaturation of A, and which structural pieces account for it?
c: 6: a benzene ring, one C=C and one C=O
5: a benzene ring and one C=O
6: a benzene ring and two C=O groups
7: a benzene ring, one C=C, one C=O and a second ring
h: Use DBE = (2C + 2 − H)/2, ignoring O. Then spend the units on what the spectra show: benzene counts 4, each other ring or π bond counts 1.
w: DBE = (2(11) + 2 − 12)/2 = 6. A benzene ring uses 4 (aromatic H at δ 7.3–7.5, four aromatic 13C signals). The single C=O (δ 167.0, IR 1712 cm−1) uses 1, and the trans CH=CH (two 1H doublets with J = 16 Hz, IR 1638 cm−1, two sp2 CH carbons at δ 144.6 and 118.3) uses the last 1. So the pieces are a benzene ring, one C=C and one C=O.
x: DBE = 5 comes from miscounting the formula (for example using H = 14). With 12 H the value is 6, and the vinyl doublets at δ 7.68/6.44 need a C=C beyond the ring and C=O.
The DBE is right but the pieces are not: the <sup>13</sup>C spectrum has only one carbonyl signal (δ 167.0); the δ 144.6 and 118.3 signals are alkene CH carbons, not a second C=O.
DBE = 7 would need H = 10. With 12 H the total is 6, and there is no evidence for an extra ring: every sp<sup>3</sup> carbon belongs to an OCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> group.

q: Unknown A, C11H12O2, gives the IR, 1H NMR and 13C NMR (with DEPT) spectra shown. The 1H doublets at δ 7.68 and 6.44 share J = 16.0 Hz. Cinnamyl acetate, CH3CO2CH2CH=CHC6H5, is an isomer of A. Which IR observation rules it out?
c: The C=O stretch at 1712 cm<sup>−1</sup> is too low for an ester whose C=O is not conjugated (1735–1750 cm<sup>−1</sup>)
There is no broad O–H band from 3300 to 2500 cm<sup>−1</sup>, so the compound is not a carboxylic acid
There is a C=C stretch at 1638 cm<sup>−1</sup>, which fits a C=C conjugated with the benzene ring
There is a strong C–O stretch at 1170 cm<sup>−1</sup>, typical of the C–O single bond of an ester
h: Both compounds are esters with a C=C. Ask which band position depends on whether the C=O is next to the C=C.
w: An ester C=O that is not conjugated absorbs at 1735–1750 cm−1; conjugation with a C=C (an α,β-unsaturated ester) lowers it to about 1715–1730 cm−1. In cinnamyl acetate the C=C is on the alcohol side, separated from the C=O by O and CH2, so its C=O would appear near 1740 cm−1. The observed 1712 cm−1 band shows a C=O conjugated with the C=C, which fits ethyl cinnamate and rules out cinnamyl acetate.
x: The missing O–H band rules out a carboxylic acid, but cinnamyl acetate has no O–H either, so this does not tell the two esters apart.
Cinnamyl acetate also contains a C=C (a styrene-type CH=CH), so a band near 1640 cm<sup>−1</sup> is expected for both isomers.
Every ester has strong C–O stretches in the 1300–1000 cm<sup>−1</sup> region, so this band appears for cinnamyl acetate too.

q: Unknown A, C11H12O2, gives the IR, 1H NMR and 13C NMR (with DEPT) spectra shown. The 1H doublets at δ 7.68 and 6.44 share J = 16.0 Hz. A is the ester shown. Which hydrogen gives the 1H doublet at δ 6.44?
c: The H on carbon a, next to the C=O
The H on carbon b, next to the ring
The para H of the benzene ring
One of the two ortho H of the benzene ring
h: In an α,β-unsaturated carbonyl, draw the resonance form that puts + charge on one alkene carbon. Which vinyl H is deshielded, and which is not?
w: Both vinyl H are 1H doublets with J = 16 Hz (trans coupling to each other). Resonance (C=C–C=O ↔ +C–C=C–O−) puts partial positive charge on the β-carbon (b), which is also next to the ring, so Hb is strongly deshielded (δ 7.68) and its carbon appears at δ 144.6. The α-carbon (a) gains electron density, so Ha, next to the C=O, is the δ 6.44 doublet (carbon at δ 118.3).
x: H<sub>b</sub> sits on the β-carbon, which carries the partial + charge in the conjugated resonance form; it is the δ 7.68 doublet, not the upfield one.
Ring H appear at δ 7.3–7.5 and overlap as multiplets; a ring H would not show a clean 16 Hz doublet far upfield at δ 6.44.
The two ortho H are equivalent, so they would integrate for 2H, and they lie near δ 7.5, not at δ 6.44 as a 1H doublet.

q: Unknown A, C11H12O2, gives the IR, 1H NMR and 13C NMR (with DEPT) spectra shown. The 1H doublets at δ 7.68 and 6.44 share J = 16.0 Hz. Which structure is A?
h: Three clues: the C=O position (conjugated or not), the ethyl group's shift (OCH<sub>2</sub> or CH<sub>2</sub> on C=O), and the J value of the vinyl doublets.
w: The quartet at δ 4.27 (2H) and triplet at δ 1.34 (3H) are an O–CH2CH3 group, so the ester is an ethyl ester. The C=O at 1712 cm−1 (and δ 167.0, typical of a conjugated ester) shows the C=O is conjugated with the C=C. The two 1H vinyl doublets with J = 16 Hz show the alkene H are trans, and the 5H aromatic multiplets show a monosubstituted ring. A is ethyl (E)-3-phenylprop-2-enoate (ethyl trans-cinnamate).
x: The (Z) isomer has the same connectivity, but cis vinyl H couple with J ≈ 12 Hz, not 16 Hz.
Cinnamyl acetate has a CH<sub>3</sub> singlet near δ 2.1 and an OCH<sub>2</sub> doublet near δ 4.7, not a quartet–triplet ethyl group; its unconjugated C=O would absorb near 1740 cm<sup>−1</sup>.
Ethyl 4-vinylbenzoate has a para ring (two 2H doublets) and a vinyl group CH=CH<sub>2</sub> (one 1H dd plus two 1H doublets near δ 5.4 and 5.9), not two 1H doublets sharing J = 16 Hz.

q: Unknown B, C6H12O, gives the IR, 1H NMR and mass spectra shown. Which process forms the even-mass fragment at m/z 58?
c: A McLafferty rearrangement: a γ-H moves to the carbonyl O and propene (42 u) is lost
An α-cleavage that breaks the bond next to the C=O and loses a propyl radical (43 u)
An α-cleavage that loses a methyl radical (15 u) from beside the C=O
Loss of water (18 u) from the molecular ion, as for an alcohol
h: Subtract 58 from the molecular ion. Is the neutral piece lost an even-mass molecule or an odd-mass radical?
w: M+ = 100, so the m/z 58 ion forms by loss of 42 u, an even-mass neutral molecule (C3H6, propene). Simple cleavages lose radicals and give odd-mass ions from an ion like this one; an even-mass ion from an even-mass M+ points to a rearrangement. For a ketone with an H on the γ-carbon this is the McLafferty rearrangement: a six-membered transition state moves the γ-H to O and breaks the α–β bond, releasing propene and leaving the enol radical cation CH2=C(OH)CH3+• (m/z 58).
x: Losing a 43 u radical from m/z 100 gives m/z 57, not 58; that cleavage accounts for the separate m/z 57 and 43 peaks.
Loss of CH<sub>3</sub> (15 u) gives m/z 85, which is a different, small peak in the spectrum.
100 − 18 = 82, and there is no peak at 82; the IR also shows no O–H band, so B is not an alcohol.

q: Unknown B, C6H12O, gives the IR, 1H NMR and mass spectra shown. B is the ketone shown. Which hydrogens give the 2H doublet at δ 2.30?
h: Match each signal by integration first, then check its splitting with the n + 1 rule.
w: The 2H integration fits only the CH2 group. Its neighbors are the C=O (no H) and one CH (1 H), so n + 1 = 2: a doublet. Being α to the C=O puts it at δ 2.30. So the δ 2.30 doublet is the CH2 on carbon b. The other signals follow: δ 2.12 (s, 3H) is CH3 a (no neighbors with H), δ 2.17 (m, 1H) is CH c (8 neighboring H), and δ 0.92 (d, 6H) is the two CH3 d groups split by the one CH.
x: CH3 a is attached to the C=O, which has no H, so it is the 3H singlet at δ 2.12, not a 2H doublet.
The CH c has 2 + 6 = 8 neighboring H, so it is the 1H multiplet at δ 2.17.
The two CH3 d groups are equivalent and integrate for 6H; they are the doublet at δ 0.92, far from the C=O.

q: Unknown B, C6H12O, gives the IR, 1H NMR and mass spectra shown. Which structure is B?
h: Use the 6H doublet and the McLafferty peak together: which isomers have an isopropyl group, and which have a γ-H for the m/z 58 ion?
w: IR 1716 cm−1 with no O–H and no aldehyde C–H pair (2720/2820 cm−1) is a saturated ketone; DBE = 1. The 3H singlet at δ 2.12 is CH3C=O, the 6H doublet at δ 0.92 is (CH3)2CH, and the 2H doublet at δ 2.30 is a CH2 between the C=O and that CH. The McLafferty ion at m/z 58 (loss of propene) needs a γ-H, which the isobutyl chain has. B is 4-methylpentan-2-one.
x: Hexan-2-one also gives m/z 58 by McLafferty, but it has a straight chain: a 2H triplet at δ 2.42 and a 3H triplet near δ 0.90, with no 6H doublet.
3-Methylpentan-2-one has a 1H sextet-like CH next to the C=O near δ 2.45, a 3H doublet and a 3H triplet; its McLafferty ion loses ethene to give m/z 72, not 58.
3,3-Dimethylbutan-2-one shows only two singlets (9H and 3H) and has no γ-H, so it cannot form a McLafferty ion at m/z 58.

q: A compound C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O<sub>2</sub> gives the IR and <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectra shown. Which structure fits?
h: Decide where the ethyl CH<sub>2</sub> is attached from its shift: next to O (δ ≈ 4.1) or next to C=O (δ ≈ 2.3).
w: IR 1740 cm−1 with no O–H is a saturated ester (DBE = 1). The 3H singlet at δ 3.67 is an O–CH3. The ethyl quartet is at δ 2.32, the shift of a CH2 on a C=O, not on O. So the ethyl group is on the acyl side: methyl propanoate, CH3CH2CO2CH3.
x: Ethyl acetate has the same three signals in a 2:3:3 ratio, but its quartet is an OCH<sub>2</sub> near δ 4.12 and its singlet is a CH<sub>3</sub>C=O near δ 2.05.
Propyl formate shows a formyl H singlet near δ 8.05 and four signals (OCH<sub>2</sub> triplet, CH<sub>2</sub> sextet, CH<sub>3</sub> triplet), not three.
2-Methylpropanoic acid would show a very broad O–H band from 3300 to 2500 cm<sup>−1</sup>, a 1H signal near δ 12 and a 6H doublet.

q: A compound C<sub>9</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O<sub>2</sub> shows a strong IR band at 1740 cm<sup>−1</sup> and the <sup>1</sup>H and <sup>13</sup>C NMR (with DEPT) spectra shown. Which structure fits?
h: Either ester orientation gives two singlets. Use the CH<sub>2</sub> carbon shift: near δ 65 when bonded to O, near δ 40 when not.
w: DBE = 5: a benzene ring and one C=O. The 1740 cm−1 band is an unconjugated ester C=O, and the 5H multiplet is a monosubstituted ring. The CH3 singlet at δ 3.69 and the CH3 carbon at δ 52.0 are a methyl ester OCH3. The CH2 singlet at δ 3.62 with its carbon at δ 41.2 is a benzylic CH2 attached to the C=O, not to O. The compound is methyl phenylacetate.
x: Benzyl acetate has the reverse ester: its OCH<sub>2</sub> is a singlet near δ 5.1 (carbon near δ 66) and its CH<sub>3</sub>C=O is near δ 2.1 (carbon near δ 21).
Ethyl benzoate has an ethyl quartet and triplet, and its C=O is conjugated with the ring (near 1720 cm<sup>−1</sup>).
Methyl 4-methylbenzoate has a para ring (two 2H doublets, 4H total) and an aryl CH<sub>3</sub> singlet near δ 2.4, with no CH<sub>2</sub> carbon.

q: A compound C<sub>9</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O<sub>2</sub> gives the IR and <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectra shown. Which structure fits?
h: Two isomers here have an ethyl group on an ester. Check the C=O band (conjugated or aryl ester) and the CH<sub>2</sub> shift.
w: DBE = 5 (ring + C=O). The C=O at 1720 cm−1 is an ester lowered by conjugation with the ring, and there is no O–H. The aromatic pattern 2H : 1H : 2H is a monosubstituted ring, and the 2H doublet at δ 8.05 is the ortho H deshielded by a C=O on the ring. The quartet at δ 4.38 is an O–CH2. The compound is ethyl benzoate.
x: Phenyl propanoate is an aryl ester: its C=O absorbs high, near 1760 cm<sup>−1</sup>, and its CH<sub>2</sub> quartet is next to C=O near δ 2.6, not at δ 4.38. Its ring H all lie near δ 7.1–7.4.
4-Ethylbenzoic acid would show a very broad O–H band (3300–2500 cm<sup>−1</sup>), a 1H signal near δ 12, and two 2H doublets for the para ring; its CH<sub>2</sub> quartet would be near δ 2.7.
4-Methoxyacetophenone shows two singlets (OCH<sub>3</sub> near δ 3.9, CH<sub>3</sub>C=O near δ 2.6), a para pattern and a ketone C=O near 1680 cm<sup>−1</sup>.

q: A compound C<sub>9</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O gives the IR and <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectra shown. Which structure fits?
h: First decide aldehyde or ketone (look near δ 9–10 and at 2720/2820 cm<sup>−1</sup>). Then use the splitting of the δ 9.81 signal to find what the CHO is attached to.
w: DBE = 5 (ring + C=O). The pair of weak bands at 2820 and 2720 cm−1 and the 1H signal at δ 9.81 show an aldehyde; the C=O at 1725 cm−1 is not conjugated. The CHO is a triplet, so it is next to a CH2. Two 2H triplets show a –CH2CH2– unit, and the 5H multiplet a monosubstituted ring. The compound is 3-phenylpropanal. (The CH2 at δ 2.78 is also split slightly by the CHO, J ≈ 1.5 Hz.)
x: Propiophenone is a ketone: no δ 9–10 signal, no 2720/2820 cm<sup>−1</sup> pair, a conjugated C=O near 1690 cm<sup>−1</sup>, and an ethyl quartet/triplet.
Phenylacetone is a ketone with two singlets (CH<sub>2</sub> near δ 3.7, CH<sub>3</sub> near δ 2.1) and no aldehyde H.
2-Phenylpropanal is an aldehyde, but its CHO is a doublet (next to a CH), and it shows a 1H quartet and a 3H doublet, not two 2H triplets.

q: A compound C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O<sub>2</sub> gives the IR, <sup>1</sup>H NMR and <sup>13</sup>C NMR spectra shown (the δ 11.9 signal disappears after a D<sub>2</sub>O shake). Which structure fits?
h: A broad band spanning 3300–2500 cm<sup>−1</sup> plus an exchangeable H near δ 12 points to one functional group. Then count <sup>13</sup>C signals.
w: The very broad O–H band, the C=O at 1708 cm−1 and the exchangeable 1H at δ 11.9 identify a carboxylic acid. Only three 13C signals for four carbons means two carbons are equivalent; the septet (1H) and 6H doublet are an isopropyl group. The compound is 2-methylpropanoic acid.
x: Butanoic acid is also an acid, but it has four different carbons (four <sup>13</sup>C signals) and shows a triplet, a sextet and a triplet.
Ethyl acetate has no O–H (no broad band, no δ 12 signal); its C=O is near 1740 cm<sup>−1</sup>.
Methyl propanoate has no O–H; its signals are a 3H singlet at δ 3.67, a quartet and a triplet.

q: A compound C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>9</sub>NO gives the IR and <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectra shown (the δ 6.25 signal disappears after a D<sub>2</sub>O shake, and the δ 2.99 doublet then becomes a singlet). Which structure fits?
h: Count the N–H bands (one or two) and ask what the CH<sub>3</sub> is coupled to, given that the doublet collapses when N–H becomes N–D.
w: DBE = 5 (ring + C=O). The C=O at 1640 cm−1 plus the 1550 cm−1 band (N–H bend) is a secondary amide, and the single N–H stretch at 3330 cm−1 shows one N–H. The CH3 is a doublet (J ≈ 5 Hz) that becomes a singlet after D2O exchange, so it is coupled to the N–H: an N–CH3 group (δ 2.99). The 2H : 3H aromatic pattern with the 2H doublet downfield at δ 7.76 is a monosubstituted ring bonded to the C=O. The compound is N-methylbenzamide.
x: 4-Methylbenzamide is a primary amide (two N–H bands near 3350 and 3180 cm<sup>−1</sup>, 2H exchangeable), with a para ring and an aryl CH<sub>3</sub> singlet near δ 2.4.
Acetanilide has one N–H, but its CH<sub>3</sub> is on the C=O: a singlet near δ 2.2 that has no N–H to couple with. Its ring H appear as 2H, 2H, 1H (δ 7.5, 7.3, 7.1).
2-Phenylacetamide is a primary amide (two N–H bands, NH<sub>2</sub>) and shows a 2H CH<sub>2</sub> singlet near δ 3.6, not a 3H doublet.

q: A compound C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>7</sub>NO gives the IR, <sup>1</sup>H NMR and <sup>13</sup>C NMR spectra shown. Which structure fits?
h: The 2220 cm<sup>−1</sup> band, the lack of an O–H band and the aromatic splitting pattern each remove one choice.
w: DBE = 6: a benzene ring (4) plus C≡N (2). The sharp band at 2220 cm−1 is a nitrile conjugated with the ring, and there is no O–H band. Two 2H doublets are a para-disubstituted ring, and the 3H singlet at δ 3.86 (carbon δ 55.5) is an aryl OCH3. Six 13C signals fit the para symmetry (δ 119.2 is the C≡N). The compound is 4-methoxybenzonitrile.
x: 3-Methoxybenzonitrile has no symmetry: four separate aromatic H signals and eight <sup>13</sup>C signals, not two 2H doublets and six carbons.
(4-Hydroxyphenyl)acetonitrile has an O–H (broad band near 3350 cm<sup>−1</sup>) and a CH<sub>2</sub> singlet near δ 3.7 (2H), not a 3H singlet.
4-(Hydroxymethyl)benzonitrile has an O–H band and a 2H CH<sub>2</sub>O singlet near δ 4.8, not a 3H singlet at δ 3.86.

q: A compound C<sub>9</sub>H<sub>13</sub>N gives the IR and <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectra shown. Which structure fits?
h: No band at 3300–3500 cm<sup>−1</sup> means no N–H. Between the tertiary amines, ask whether the N is on the ring or on a CH<sub>2</sub>.
w: DBE = 4, a benzene ring. There is no N–H stretch, so the amine is tertiary. The 5H multiplet near δ 7.3 is a monosubstituted ring that is not attached to N (an N on the ring pushes the ortho/para H upfield to δ 6.6–6.8). The 2H singlet at δ 3.42 is a benzylic CH2 on N, and the 6H singlet at δ 2.24 is N(CH3)2. The compound is N,N-dimethylbenzylamine.
x: N-Ethyl-N-methylaniline is also tertiary, but it has an ethyl quartet/triplet, an N–CH<sub>3</sub> singlet near δ 2.9 (3H), and ring H split 2H : 3H with the ortho/para H near δ 6.7.
4-Isopropylaniline is a primary amine with two N–H bands near 3430 and 3350 cm<sup>−1</sup>, a para ring (two 2H doublets), a septet and a 6H doublet.
N-Methyl-2-phenylethylamine is a secondary amine (one N–H band) and shows two 2H triplets plus a 3H singlet.

q: A compound C<sub>9</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O gives the IR and <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectra shown. Which structure fits?
h: Two isomers here have a para ring, an ethyl and a methyl. Which one, the CH<sub>2</sub> or the CH<sub>3</sub>, is on the oxygen? Compare δ 3.99 with δ 2.28.
w: DBE = 4 (a benzene ring); no O–H band, so the O is an ether (strong aryl C–O at 1245 cm−1). Two 2H doublets are a para ring. The quartet is at δ 3.99, the shift of an O–CH2, and the 3H singlet at δ 2.28 is an aryl CH3. So the ethyl is on O and the methyl is on the ring: 1-ethoxy-4-methylbenzene.
x: 4-Ethylanisole has the same signal pattern, but its O–CH<sub>3</sub> singlet is near δ 3.78 and its benzylic CH<sub>2</sub> quartet is near δ 2.6.
1-Ethoxy-2-methylbenzene is ortho-disubstituted: four different aromatic H that appear as a multiplet, not two 2H doublets.
1-(4-Methylphenyl)ethanol has an O–H (broad band near 3350 cm<sup>−1</sup>, exchangeable 1H), a 1H quartet near δ 4.85 and a 3H doublet near δ 1.47.

q: A compound C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O<sub>3</sub> gives the IR, <sup>1</sup>H NMR and <sup>13</sup>C NMR (with DEPT) spectra shown. The δ 10.76 signal is sharp and disappears after a D<sub>2</sub>O shake. Which structure fits?
h: Four 1H aromatic signals limit the substitution pattern. Methyl ester CH<sub>3</sub> (carbon near δ 52) or aryl ether (near δ 56)? Does the O–H look like an acid's?
w: DBE = 5 (ring + C=O). Four different 1H aromatic signals (d, t, d, t) mean an ortho-disubstituted ring. The CH3 carbon at δ 52.2 is a methyl ester OCH3, not an aryl ether. The O–H is a band near 3190 cm−1 without the 3300–2500 cm−1 sprawl of an acid, and its sharp δ 10.76 signal is a phenol O–H held downfield by an intramolecular hydrogen bond to the ester C=O; that same hydrogen bond and conjugation lower the C=O to 1680 cm−1. The compound is methyl 2-hydroxybenzoate (methyl salicylate).
x: Methyl 4-hydroxybenzoate is para (two 2H doublets, six <sup>13</sup>C signals), and its phenol O–H, with no intramolecular hydrogen bond, is a broad signal near δ 6, not a sharp δ 10.76 singlet.
4-Methoxybenzoic acid is para (two 2H doublets), shows a very broad 3300–2500 cm<sup>−1</sup> acid O–H, and its aryl OCH<sub>3</sub> carbon is near δ 55.5.
2-Methoxybenzoic acid is also ortho, but its CH<sub>3</sub> is an aryl ether (carbon near δ 56) and its acid O–H gives a very broad 3300–2500 cm<sup>−1</sup> IR band.

q: A compound C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O gives the IR and <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectra shown. The vinyl signals at δ 6.85 and 6.10 share J = 16 Hz. Which structure fits?
h: A C=O near 1675 cm<sup>−1</sup> is lower than a normal ketone. What lowers it, and does the spectrum show an aldehyde H?
w: DBE = 2: one C=O and one C=C. The C=O at 1675 cm−1 (about 40 cm−1 below a saturated ketone) and the C=C at 1635 cm−1 show an α,β-unsaturated ketone. There is no aldehyde H. The CH3 singlet at δ 2.25 is CH3C=O; the 3H doublet at δ 1.90 is a CH3 on the alkene, split by the vinyl H at δ 6.85 (a multiplet, coupled to both the other vinyl H and the CH3). J = 16 Hz and the 970 cm−1 band fit a trans alkene. The compound is (E)-pent-3-en-2-one.
x: Cyclopentanone has no C=C or vinyl H; its C=O is raised by ring strain to about 1745 cm<sup>−1</sup>, and its <sup>1</sup>H spectrum is two 4H signals near δ 2.0–2.2.
Pent-4-en-2-one is not conjugated: its C=O stays near 1715 cm<sup>−1</sup>, and it shows a terminal =CH<sub>2</sub> (2H near δ 5.1) and a CH<sub>2</sub> doublet near δ 3.2.
(E)-Pent-2-enal is an aldehyde: a 1H doublet near δ 9.5 and the C–H pair near 2720/2820 cm<sup>−1</sup>, with an ethyl group instead of two CH<sub>3</sub> signals.

q: A compound C<sub>9</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O<sub>2</sub> gives the IR and <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectra shown (the δ 11.2 signal disappears after a D<sub>2</sub>O shake). Which structure fits?
h: Identify the functional group from the broad IR band and δ 11.2, then read the CH/CH<sub>3</sub> splitting.
w: The very broad O–H band (3300–2500 cm−1), the C=O at 1705 cm−1 and the exchangeable 1H at δ 11.2 identify a carboxylic acid. DBE = 5 (ring + C=O), and the 5H multiplet is a monosubstituted ring. A 1H quartet and a 3H doublet are a CH–CH3 unit, with the CH (δ 3.74) both benzylic and α to the C=O. The compound is 2-phenylpropanoic acid.
x: 3-Phenylpropanoic acid has a –CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>– chain: two 2H triplets near δ 2.95 and 2.68, not a quartet and a doublet.
4-Ethylbenzoic acid has a para ring (two 2H doublets) and an ethyl group: a 2H quartet near δ 2.7 and a 3H triplet.
Methyl phenylacetate is an ester with no O–H band and no δ 11 signal; it shows two singlets (OCH<sub>3</sub> and CH<sub>2</sub>).

q: A compound C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>7</sub>ClO<sub>2</sub> shows a strong IR band at 1750 cm<sup>−1</sup> and gives the mass spectrum and <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum shown. Which structure fits?
h: All four choices are chloro esters with M<sup>+</sup> 122/124. Use the multiplicities and integrations, then the shift of the quartet: is that CH<sub>2</sub> on O or on Cl?
w: M+ at 122 and M+2 at 124 in a 3:1 ratio show one Cl; 1750 cm−1 is an ester C=O made slightly higher by the α-Cl. The quartet (2H, δ 4.24) and triplet (3H, δ 1.30) are an O–CH2CH3, so the ester is an ethyl ester. The remaining 2H singlet at δ 4.06 is a CH2 between Cl and C=O with no neighbors. The acylium ion ClCH2CO+ (m/z 77/79, 3:1, from loss of ·OCH2CH3) fits. The compound is ethyl chloroacetate.
x: Methyl 3-chloropropanoate has an OCH<sub>3</sub> singlet (3H) and two 2H triplets (ClCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>), with no quartet; its acylium ion would be at m/z 91/93.
2-Chloroethyl acetate has a CH<sub>3</sub>C=O singlet near δ 2.1 (3H) and two 2H triplets for OCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Cl; its base peak would be CH<sub>3</sub>CO<sup>+</sup> at m/z 43.
Methyl 2-chloropropanoate gives a quartet, a singlet and a doublet, but in a 1H : 3H : 3H ratio (CHCl near δ 4.4, OCH<sub>3</sub>, CH<sub>3</sub> doublet), not 2H : 2H : 3H.

q: A compound C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O<sub>3</sub> gives the IR, <sup>1</sup>H NMR and <sup>13</sup>C NMR (with DEPT) spectra shown. Which structure fits?
h: Two carbonyl carbons (δ 206 and 173) mean a ketone plus an ester. All four choices have 2H, 2H, 3H, 3H integrations, so the multiplicities decide.
w: DBE = 2: two C=O groups, a ketone (δ 206.6, IR 1717 cm−1) and an ester (δ 173.2, IR 1738 cm−1). The CH3 singlet at δ 3.67 (carbon δ 51.7) is a methyl ester OCH3; the CH3 singlet at δ 2.19 (carbon δ 29.8) is CH3C=O. Two 2H triplets are a –CH2CH2– unit with a carbonyl on each end (both near δ 2.6–2.8). The compound is methyl 4-oxopentanoate.
x: Ethyl acetoacetate has an ethyl ester (2H quartet near δ 4.2, 3H triplet) and an isolated CH<sub>2</sub> singlet near δ 3.4 between the two C=O groups, not two triplets.
Methyl 3-oxopentanoate has a CH<sub>2</sub> singlet near δ 3.45 between the two C=O groups and an ethyl quartet/triplet on the ketone, not two triplets and two singlets.
Methyl 5-oxopentanoate is an aldehyde: a 1H triplet near δ 9.8 and a CHO carbon near δ 202 (a CH in DEPT), with no CH<sub>3</sub>C=O singlet.

q: A compound C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>9</sub>NO gives the IR and <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectra shown (the δ 3.42 signal disappears after a D<sub>2</sub>O shake). Which structure fits?
h: Two sharp-ish N–H bands mean one kind of amine. The aromatic pattern and the 3H singlet do the rest.
w: DBE = 4, a benzene ring. Two N–H bands at 3425 and 3345 cm−1 (symmetric and asymmetric stretches) and an exchangeable 2H signal mean a primary amine, NH2. Two 2H doublets are a para ring, shifted upfield (δ 6.6–6.8) by two electron-donating groups. The 3H singlet at δ 3.75 with the strong 1235 cm−1 aryl C–O band is an OCH3. The compound is 4-methoxyaniline.
x: 4-Aminobenzyl alcohol has an O–H (broad band) and a 2H CH<sub>2</sub>O singlet near δ 4.5, not a 3H singlet near δ 3.75.
2-Methoxyaniline has the same groups but ortho: four different aromatic H as a multiplet, not two 2H doublets.
4-(Methylamino)phenol has one N–H and an O–H (a broad O–H band, not two sharp N–H bands) and an N–CH<sub>3</sub> singlet near δ 2.8.

q: A compound C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O gives the IR, <sup>1</sup>H NMR and <sup>13</sup>C NMR (with DEPT) spectra shown. The vinyl signals at δ 6.98 and 6.01 share J = 10 Hz. Which structure fits?
h: Use the C=O position for conjugation, the vinyl CH carbons for how many H sit on the C=C, and each vinyl carbon's shift to find the β-carbon.
w: DBE = 3: C=O + C=C + one ring. The C=O at 1680 cm−1 and δ 199.9 (below the δ 205–212 of a saturated ketone) show conjugation with the C=C (1620 cm−1). DEPT shows two alkene CH carbons, and the β-carbon is strongly deshielded (δ 151.0) by resonance with the C=O, while the α-carbon is at δ 129.9. There is no aldehyde H, and three CH2 groups complete a six-membered ring. J = 10 Hz fits cis vinyl H in a ring. The compound is cyclohex-2-en-1-one.
x: Cyclohex-3-en-1-one is not conjugated: its C=O would be near 1715 cm<sup>−1</sup> and δ 209, and both vinyl carbons would be near δ 125, with no strongly deshielded β-carbon.
Cyclopent-1-ene-1-carbaldehyde is an aldehyde: a 1H singlet near δ 9.8 and only one vinyl H (its other alkene carbon has no H).
2-Methylcyclopent-2-en-1-one has only one vinyl H and a CH<sub>3</sub> singlet near δ 1.8; DEPT would show one alkene CH and a CH<sub>3</sub>, not two alkene CH.

q: A compound C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O shows a strong IR band at 1715 cm<sup>−1</sup> and gives the <sup>1</sup>H and <sup>13</sup>C NMR spectra shown. Which structure fits?
h: Five carbons but only three <sup>13</sup>C signals: look for the symmetric choice.
w: DBE = 1 and 1715 cm−1 with δ 211.8 is a saturated ketone. Five carbons giving only three 13C signals, and only two 1H signals (4H quartet, 6H triplet), mean two identical ethyl groups on the C=O. The compound is pentan-3-one.
x: Pentan-2-one has no symmetry: five <sup>13</sup>C signals and four <sup>1</sup>H signals, including a CH<sub>3</sub>C=O singlet near δ 2.1.
Pentanal is an aldehyde: a 1H triplet near δ 9.8, a CHO carbon near δ 202 and five <sup>13</sup>C signals.
2-Methylbutanal is an aldehyde with five different carbons and a 1H doublet near δ 9.6.

q: A compound C<sub>9</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O<sub>2</sub> gives the IR and <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectra shown. Which structure fits?
h: All of these have two CH<sub>3</sub> groups. Look at where neither singlet is (δ 3.8–3.9), and at how high the C=O band is.
w: DBE = 5 (ring + C=O). Two 2H doublets are a para ring. Neither CH3 singlet is near δ 3.9, so there is no OCH3: δ 2.33 and 2.28 are an aryl CH3 and a CH3C=O. A C=O at 1765 cm−1 is higher than an alkyl ester (≈1740 cm−1), the mark of a phenyl ester, where the ring pulls the O lone pair away from the C=O. The ring H are fairly upfield (no C=O on the ring). The compound is 4-methylphenyl acetate.
x: Methyl 4-methylbenzoate has the ester reversed: an OCH<sub>3</sub> singlet near δ 3.9, a ring doublet near δ 7.9 (ortho to C=O), and a conjugated C=O near 1720 cm<sup>−1</sup>.
4-Methoxyacetophenone has an OCH<sub>3</sub> singlet near δ 3.9, a ring doublet near δ 7.9, and a conjugated ketone C=O near 1680 cm<sup>−1</sup>.
2-Methylphenyl acetate is also an aryl ester (C=O near 1765 cm<sup>−1</sup>), but it is ortho-disubstituted: four different aromatic H as a multiplet, not two 2H doublets.
